source: Eisape, Tessler, Dasgupta, Sha, van Steenkiste, Linzen (2024) A Systematic Comparison of Syllogistic Reasoning in Humans and Language Models
finding: On all 64 syllogism types, PaLM 2 models (zero-shot chain of thought) beat humans on average and larger models were more accurate. Even the best model was only about 75% accurate. Scale did not give steady gains: the largest model scored a bit lower than the second largest.
numbers: 64 syllogisms (27 with a valid quantified conclusion, 37 where 'nothing follows'). Human average about 50%. Best LM about 75%. Llama 2 replication: accuracy near human level, small rise with size.
quote: larger models are more logical than smaller ones, and also more logical than humans
limits: Accuracy is scored on the 27 syllogisms with a valid conclusion only. Zero-shot CoT prompt. One model family plus a Llama 2 replication.
agent_relevance: Baseline: a strong model is not a reliable syllogism solver. Do not assume bigger means logical; any syllogism step in S4 needs a check.

source: Eisape et al. (2024), figural and fallacy analyses
finding: Models copy two human biases. They are sensitive to the irrelevant order of terms (A-B/B-C versus B-A/C-B, the figural effect). They give confident wrong answers on the same fallacy syllogisms that fool people (for example, no A are B and all B are C gives 'no A are C'). Larger models were somewhat more susceptible to these fallacies. On some syllogisms (EA1) accuracy fell as model size grew.
numbers: Response distributions correlate fairly highly with human distributions across models; correlation is highest for PaLM 2 Small. Accuracy is inversely related to response entropy (confident errors on fallacies).
limits: Better fit to humans partly offsets miscalibration from higher accuracy; correlation does not prove the same mechanism.
agent_relevance: Test items for S4 should include figure-swapped twins of the same syllogism. A disagreement between the two orderings is a free, code-checkable inconsistency signal (fits G1, G3).

source: Eisape et al. (2024), 'nothing follows' behavior and mReasoner fit
finding: Models almost never answer 'nothing follows', which is correct for 37 of 64 syllogisms. Accuracy on that answer is close to 0% under the zero-shot CoT generative prompt, a much stronger aversion than humans show. A binary yes/no discrimination format (appendix B.3) gets markedly higher accuracy on these cases. Fitting the mReasoner mental-model simulator suggested larger LMs reason more deliberatively.
numbers: Accuracy on 'nothing follows' near 0% (Figure 6). mReasoner grid: 923 finished simulations; first principal component (77% of variance) correlates with accuracy.
limits: Authors leave the cause for future work. The system-2 reading is a model fit, not direct evidence.
agent_relevance: Ask 'does this specific conclusion follow, yes or no' for each candidate rather than 'what follows'. A code loop over the eight candidate conclusions with one binary question each targets the missing-NVC failure.

source: Bertolazzi, Gatt, Bernardi (2024) A Systematic Analysis of Large Language Models as Soft Reasoners: The Case of Syllogistic Inferences
finding: Zero-shot CoT on Pythia and LLaMA models: accuracy on valid syllogisms rose with size, but accuracy on invalid ones (correct answer 'nothing follows') stayed far below human level. Instruction tuning helped invalid items but cost accuracy on valid items. When the true conclusion is unbelievable, most models dropped in accuracy.
numbers: Humans: 44.63% valid, 40.97% invalid. LLaMA-3 8B-inst: 50.00 overall, 78.15 valid, 30.28 invalid. LLaMA-3 70B-inst: 41.25 overall, 54.44 valid, 32.50 invalid. LLaMA-3 70B base 30.63 overall. Pythia-1.4B 14.22 overall. Valid-schema items: 27 schemas x 10 term triples = 270.
limits: Small open models only. Generative multiple-choice with nine options. Human figures are the Khemlani and Johnson-Laird (2012) aggregate.
agent_relevance: Instruction tuning trades valid-item accuracy for invalid-item accuracy. Our harness should score valid and invalid items separately, never one accuracy number.

source: Bertolazzi et al. (2024), in-context learning versus fine-tuning
finding: In-context examples did not teach models to say 'nothing follows', even when the examples were of the same schema as the test item. Supervised fine-tuning fixed it. Fine-tuning removed content effects only with pseudo-word terms. In-context learning made models give more contradictory answers. More premises (3 or 4 chained) made zero-shot CoT worse.
numbers: Contradictory answers: LLaMA-3 8B zero-shot CoT 1.09%, Pythia 18.91%. SFT on Pythia: 73.91% contradictory, of which 70.47% came from adding 'nothing follows' beside another conclusion. 28 schemas with an A-premise x 10 term sets = 280 items per length.
limits: SFT is not available to us (the agent is scaffold-only). Small models.
agent_relevance: Few-shot demonstrations are not a fix for the 'nothing follows' gap. This favors a code-side enumeration check over more prompt examples.

source: Bertolazzi et al. (2024), heuristic-theory fit
finding: The atmosphere heuristic fits LLaMA-3 zero-shot CoT output very well. It predicts the model's errors on invalid and valid schemas and its correct conclusions. Conversion theory fits less well. So much of the model's apparent syllogism 'reasoning' looks like mood matching.
numbers: Atmosphere predicts 92.31% of correct valid conclusions, 82.97% of errors on invalid schemas, 62.79% of errors on valid schemas. For humans, atmosphere predicts 62.50% of correct valid conclusions and 0% on invalid. Conversion predicts 58.33% (LLaMA-3) and 50.70% (Pythia) of mistakes.
limits: Fit for a base model with zero-shot CoT; measures how many outputs a heuristic can predict, not a causal test.
agent_relevance: Heuristic answers are detectable in code: if the output equals the atmosphere prediction and a validity check disagrees, flag it. Gives G1 a concrete trigger.

source: Lampinen, Dasgupta, Chan, Sheahan, Creswell, Kumaran, McClelland, Hill (2024) Language models show human-like content effects on reasoning tasks
finding: On syllogism validity, natural language inference and the Wason task, language models show the same direction of content effect as humans: better when logic and belief agree. Held for Chinchilla, PaLM 2-M and L, Flan-PaLM 2 and GPT-3.5. A few examples took Chinchilla from content-biased to near ceiling on NLI, and a simple instruction cut bias. Few-shot examples gave mild gains on harder tasks but did not remove content effects.
numbers: Belief-by-validity interaction significant in humans, PaLM 2-L, Flan-PaLM 2 and GPT-3.5 (all z > 5.9); not significant in Chinchilla or PaLM 2-M. Realistic-content advantage on Wason significant in humans, Chinchilla, PaLM 2-L, GPT-3.5 (z > 2.2, p < 0.03).
quote: a unitary language model may mirror this dual behavior in humans
limits: Likelihood scoring and answer format change raw accuracy; GPT-3.5 and Chinchilla were biased toward answering 'valid' in the nonsense condition. Overlaps with the content-effects file in this series.
agent_relevance: Abstract-form restatement (swap terms to nonsense words) before judging, then compare verdicts on both versions (G3, mutated input).

source: Zong and Lin (2024) Categorical Syllogisms Revisited: A Review of the Logical Reasoning Abilities of LLMs
finding: Review of syllogism benchmarks. Synthetic template datasets cover all mood-and-figure configurations but have little language variety. Crowdsourced datasets have more variety but miss many configurations. Across prior work, models score around 75% when judging validity. Error breakdown by mood and figure points to quantifier interpretation as the main bottleneck.
numbers: GPT-4 proposition translation: 87.3% correct on 371 textbook problems. On 116 textbook items a model-based pipeline gets mood detection 87.9%, figure 48.3%, full configuration 44.8%. 256 mood-figure configurations in the Reasoning dataset.
limits: Review plus a small own analysis on GPT-4 and GPT-4o. Cross-checking against valid-form lists is a heuristic.
agent_relevance: A cheap structural check exists: parse mood and figure, then look the pair up in the table of valid forms (24 traditional, 15 without existential import). That is a code check usable at S4.

source: Zong and Lin (2024), existential import and quantifiers
finding: Existential import is a hidden choice in benchmarks. Some valid-form lists assume traditional logic (All A are B implies some A exist) and others modern logic. Datasets rarely state which. Models also err on how they read 'all', 'some' and generalized quantifiers (few, most).
numbers: The paper discusses 9 cases that rely on existential import.
limits: Discussion is partly qualitative.
agent_relevance: The agent must be told which reading holds before judging a syllogism. Make it an explicit S0 restatement field, not an implicit default.

source: Zang et al. (2026) A Syllogistic Probe: Tracing the Evolution of Logic Reasoning in Large Language Models
finding: Using existential import as a probe, bigger models shift from the traditional-logic reading (some A exist) to the modern reading. Thinking variants shift further than same-size instruct variants. Base model matters: Gemma and Llama base models often answer 'invalid' by default and miss modern-valid forms. A CoT trigger gave only a limited shift. A prior-check prompt (check assumptions first) consistently raised modern-logic accuracy.
numbers: Qwen3-8B instruct still mostly traditional; Qwen3-8B-Thinking moves clearly to modern. Qwen family 0.6B to 235B. Modern logic accepts 15 moods, traditional 24.
limits: Which logic is right depends on the benchmark; the paper measures alignment, not truth. Exact accuracy values are in tables I did not extract.
agent_relevance: A benchmark score on a syllogism set may reflect the logic reading, not skill. Pin the reading in the prompt; a 'state your assumptions first' step is a candidate S0 operator to test at equal tokens (G7).

source: Poddar, Sahoo, Ghosh (2025) Understanding Syllogistic Reasoning in LLMs from Formal and Natural Language Perspectives
finding: 14 LLMs, four prompting strategies (zero-shot, one-shot, few-shot, zero-shot CoT), three temperatures, 160 syllogisms. Mean accuracy on logical validity is far above agreement with real-world believability, because strong models judge validity regardless of belief. Belief bias (congruent minus incongruent accuracy) is positive in 12 of 14 models; top models under 2 points, weak models up to about 47. Higher reasoning ability goes with lower bias.
numbers: 26,880 evaluations. Syntax accuracy mean 81.7% (SD 17.1) vs believability agreement 56.2%. Mean bias +10.81 points (p = 0.028, d = 0.66). Best: Gemini 2.5 Flash 99.6%. Worst: Llama 3.2 1B 51.9%. Bias-ability correlation -0.565. Dataset: 76 valid, 84 invalid; 82 congruent, 78 incongruent.
limits: Small item set (160), only 38 believable conclusions. Includes nonsense-word and premise-swap variants. 14-model sample.
agent_relevance: Belief bias is now mostly a weak-model problem. Measure it on our own model with matched pairs before adding any fix.

source: Poddar et al. (2025), precision and recall pattern
finding: Models with similar accuracy can err in opposite ways. One model had 99.2% precision but 42.8% recall (rejects valid items). Gemma 3 27B IT had 93.1% recall but 61.0% precision (accepts too much).
numbers: Six models above 95% syntax accuracy. Consistency across four variants near 99% for the best.
limits: Per model and prompt; may shift with wording.
agent_relevance: Track precision and recall on valid and invalid items separately. A single accuracy figure hides an acceptance bias that a vote cannot repair.

source: Ando, Morishita, Abe, Mineshima, Okada (2023) Evaluating Large Language Models with NeuBAROCO: Syllogistic Reasoning Ability and Human-like Biases
finding: Bilingual English and Japanese syllogism set built from psychology experiments (BAROCO). Models do worse on problems that trigger belief bias, conversion errors (reading 'all A are B' as 'all B are A') and atmosphere effects.
numbers: Numbers are in the 2024 follow-up (c14).
limits: I read the abstract and introduction of this version only.
agent_relevance: Conversion and atmosphere are named, countable error types. Our S4 error taxonomy can use them as labels.

source: Ozeki, Ando, Morishita, Abe, Mineshima, Okada (2024) Exploring Reasoning Biases in Large Language Models Through Syllogism: NeuBAROCO
finding: GPT-4 is far stronger than GPT-3.5 and Llama-2. Accuracy is lower on belief-incongruent, conversion and atmosphere items. The 'neutral' label (neither entailment nor contradiction) is hardest: GPT-4 scores about 30 points lower there, often answering 'contradiction'. Translating the syllogism into abstract logic first and then explaining showed the main limit is the reasoning step, not reading the sentences.
numbers: Multiple-choice (80 problems), English: GPT-4 83.75, GPT-3.5 53.75, Llama-2-70B 56.25; Japanese: GPT-4 95.00, GPT-3.5 42.50; humans 53.00. NLI (790 items), English GPT-4 zero-shot-row 77.47 overall. Translate-and-explain (90 problems): predicate-logic translation correct 87/90 (GPT-4 English), 82/90 (GPT-3.5); set-theory 82/90 and 79/90; Japanese GPT-3.5 set-theory only 28/90.
limits: Closed models, small sets, translation checked by hand. GPT-3.5 misread scope of negation in 'some A are not B'.
agent_relevance: Translation to formal form is nearly error-free for GPT-4 while judging is not. So the weak step is inference, and a solver can take over after translation (see Logic-LM, c18).

source: Wang and Shi (2025) Logical forms complement probability in understanding language model (and human) performance
finding: Hypothetical (conditional) and disjunctive syllogisms in propositional and modal logic. Argument form predicts LLM accuracy beyond input probability. Modus tollens is the hardest valid form; modus ponens the easiest. Lower input perplexity goes with higher accuracy in every model. Few-shot demos raise scores, partly by copying answers.
numbers: Estimated marginal means of soft accuracy on valid sequents: modus ponens 0.59, disjunctive 0.54, modus tollens 0.31 (all pairwise p < 0.001). Modality: 'may' 0.61, propositional 0.55, 'must' 0.27. Mixed-effects marginal R2 0.342, conditional R2 0.543.
limits: Soft accuracy from model probabilities, open models of several sizes. A human comparison exists but I did not extract it.
agent_relevance: Same asymmetry as in people (MT harder than MP). A contrapositive rewrite (if not q then not p) before judging MT items is a cheap operator to test.

source: Holliday, Mandelkern, Zhang (2024) Conditional and Modal Reasoning in Large Language Models
finding: 29 LLMs on valid and invalid conditional, disjunctive and modal inference patterns. All models commit basic fallacies. Even the best are inconsistent across some patterns, and many differ from human judgment on complex conditional inferences. Zero-shot chain of thought improves accuracy a lot (best models near 90%) but errors remain. Pattern accuracy tracks Chatbot Arena Elo, MMLU and GSM8K.
numbers: 29 models; 20 instances per pattern; chance 50%; zero-shot accuracy on basic patterns ranges from about 45% to 89% across models; CoT gain significant (paired t-test).
quote: all models commit basic fallacies in reasoning with modals and conditionals
limits: Yes/no validity on hand-built instances. They reject the material-conditional reading, so some 'errors' depend on a theoretical stance.
agent_relevance: A benchmark design to copy: 20 instances per pattern, nonsense-word twins, zero-shot versus CoT. Supports a per-pattern consistency check for S4.

source: Holliday et al. (2024), overgeneralizing modus tollens and modal substitution
finding: Many models overgeneralize valid Boolean patterns (MP, MT, disjunctive syllogism) to modal cases where the pattern fails. Some reject MT with 'might not' but accept the equivalent MT with 'not must', which is inconsistent. The best models all accepted the contested conditional-modus-ponens pattern (CMP) zero-shot, against human judgment. CoT cut this but not to human levels.
numbers: Top zero-shot models uniformly accept CMP; about 90% accuracy only with CoT.
limits: Which answer is correct for MTmu, DSmu and CMP is debated in semantics.
agent_relevance: Equivalent-wording consistency (same logic, two phrasings) is a code-checkable test needing no ground truth; use it as an impasse trigger.

source: Pan, Albalak, Wang, Wang (2023) Logic-LM: Empowering Large Language Models with Symbolic Solvers for Faithful Logical Reasoning
finding: The LLM only translates the problem into a symbolic form; a solver (logic programming, FOL prover, constraint or SAT solver) does the inference; the answer is read from the solver output. This beat standard prompting and chain of thought on four of five logic benchmarks. Self-refinement from solver error messages added small gains where translation failed.
numbers: Average gain 39.2% over standard prompting and 18.4% over CoT (GPT-3.5, abstract). GPT-4 standard / CoT / Logic-LM: ProofWriter 52.67 / 68.11 / 79.66; FOLIO 69.11 / 70.58 / 78.92; LogicalDeduction 71.33 / 75.25 / 87.63; PrOntoQA 77.40 / 98.79 / 83.20 (solver worse); AR-LSAT 33.33 / 35.06 / 43.04. FOLIO executable rate about 79.9% before refinement for GPT-4.
limits: PrOntoQA shows CoT can beat the pipeline when translation is lossy. No syllogism-only set. 600 sampled examples per dataset.
agent_relevance: Direct template for an S4 solver operator: model writes the formal form, program decides. Needs a fallback to the plain answer when the solver fails (G6).

source: Olausson, Gu, Lipkin, Zhang, Solar-Lezama, Tenenbaum, Levy (2023) LINC: A Neurosymbolic Approach for Logical Reasoning by Combining Language Models with First-Order Logic Provers
finding: LLM acts as a semantic parser to first-order logic; a theorem prover deduces; ten parses are majority-voted. LINC helped a small 15.5B model a lot and helped GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 on a balanced ProofWriter subset, but did not beat chain of thought for GPT-4 on FOLIO. The two methods fail on different items. Most LINC failures are in the parse (syntax errors, missing background facts, mismatched predicates).
numbers: ProofWriter: GPT-4 with LINC 98.3%, GPT-3.5 with LINC 96.4%; StarCoder+ with LINC beat GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 CoT by absolute 38% and 10%. FOLIO: StarCoder+ LINC 56.0% vs 41.8% CoT; GPT-4 LINC vs CoT not significant (McNemar p = 0.58). StarCoder+ parse syntax errors 38%. K = 10 majority vote.
limits: Gains depend on synthetic, short, regular text (ProofWriter). Real-world FOLIO text breaks parsing.
agent_relevance: The ten-way parse vote is code-side (G5), but parse errors are correlated model errors (G4): voting cannot detect a shared misreading of 'some' or 'all'.

source: Akinfaderin and Diallo (2026) FregeLogic at SemEval-2026 Task 11: A Hybrid Neuro-Symbolic Architecture for Content-Robust Syllogistic Validity Prediction
finding: Five LLM classifiers (three open models, four prompt styles) vote on syllogism validity. The Z3 solver is consulted only on narrow 3-2 splits. This cut the content effect by 16% and added 0.9 points of accuracy. Z3 alone, or Z3 as a veto, was far worse because the LLM step that extracts the structure fails or errs.
numbers: N = 960, nested 5-fold. Tiebreaker: accuracy 94.3 +/- 0.9, content effect 2.85 +/- 1.23, combined score 41.88 +/- 5.97. Z3 weighting: 93.4, 3.39, 39.12. Z3 only: 74.7, 26.28, 17.39. Z3 veto: 74.1, 26.70, 17.18. Structured-output extraction cut Z3 parse failure from 22% to near zero.
limits: The 2.76-point score gain is small against the 5.97 spread. Shared-task data and its own metric.
agent_relevance: Design rule: call the formal solver only when attempts disagree (matches G1). Never let a solver fed by an LLM parse override a strong consensus. Use structured output for extraction.

source: Valentino, Kim, Dalal, Zhao, Freitas (2026) Mitigating Content Effects on Reasoning in Language Models Through Fine-Grained Activation Steering
finding: Prompting alone, including chain of thought, does not remove content effects in syllogistic validity. Activation steering at localized layers can reduce them. A conditional version that sets strength per input gave up to 15% absolute gain in formal accuracy on models unresponsive to static steering. Vectors from synthetic data transferred with variation across models.
numbers: Up to 15% absolute improvement; robust to prompt variations; small side effects on language modeling.
limits: Needs open-weight access to activations; generalization partial. I read abstract, introduction and summary text.
agent_relevance: Not usable in a prompt-only scaffold. Recorded so we do not expect prompt tricks to remove content effects completely.

source: Wysocka, Carvalho, Wysocki, Valentino, Freitas (2025) SylloBio-NLI: Evaluating Large Language Models on Biomedical Syllogistic Reasoning
finding: Syllogistic schemes instantiated with biomedical facts (28 pathways). Zero-shot average accuracy ranged from 70% on generalized modus ponens to 23% on disjunctive syllogism (chance 50%, so disjunctive is below chance). Few-shot examples raised F1 for Gemma by 14% and Llama-3 by 43%, but both settings are sensitive to lexical changes.
numbers: 7 general schemes. Best open model Gemma-7B-it 64% (task 1) and 55% (task 2) zero-shot. Few-shot F1 gains +14% (Gemma-7B) and +43% (Llama-3-8B).
limits: Small 7B-8B open models. Domain terms from an ontology.
agent_relevance: Scores differ sharply by schema, so aggregate numbers hide the weak form. Break the harness down per schema (MP, MT, DS).

source: Ye, Kuribayashi, Suzuki, Kobayashi, Funayama (2023) Assessing Step-by-Step Reasoning against Lexical Negation: A Case Study on Syllogism
finding: Dozens of LLMs reasoning step by step over fictional-entity syllogisms break when one predicate is replaced by its lexical negation (plausible to implausible). Performance falls drastically for many models, even GPT-3.5 and LLaMA-65B, also when exemplars contain negation. Model families fail in different ways.
numbers: Models: GPT-4, GPT-3.5, LLaMA 7B-65B, Vicuna, OPT 6.7B-175B, BLOOM, BLOOMZ. GPT-4 stays high in most conditions; many others fall toward 50% or a constant answer.
limits: Lexical negation only (not syntactic 'not'); fictional entities; 2023 models. Exact per-condition values not transcribed.
agent_relevance: Negation hurts models as it hurts people on MT and DA items. A restatement that removes lexical negation (use 'not plausible') is a candidate S0 operator.

source: Abe, Ando, Morishita, Ozeki, Mineshima, Okada (2026) Abductive Reasoning with Syllogistic Forms in Large Language Models
finding: Reversing the syllogism task (given major premise and conclusion, find the minor premise) is much harder than deduction. GPT-4 zero-shot abduction is barely above chance while deduction on the same items is far higher. Few-shot examples help deduction more than abduction. Belief-inconsistent items are about 10 points worse.
numbers: n = 216 items. GPT-4 zero-shot: abduction about 42%, deduction 72.22%; few-shot deduction 95.83%. Llama-3-70B few-shot: abduction 75.46%, deduction 84.72%.
limits: Translated syllogism set with fixed answer options.
agent_relevance: Going from conclusion back to cause (affirming-the-consequent direction) is the weak direction. The agent should label such steps as hypotheses, not conclusions.

source: Abe, Ozeki, Ando, Morishita, Mineshima, Okada (2026) Evaluation of Deontic Conditional Reasoning in Large Language Models: The Case of Wason's Selection Task
finding: New Wason dataset separating deontic rules (permission, obligation) from descriptive rules. Every model and prompt type (zero-shot, few-shot, CoT) is more accurate on deontic rules, by 5.0 to 41.2 points. Selection patterns fit matching bias better than confirmation bias. Matching on q for a false consequent is logically valid, so matching does not always lower accuracy.
numbers: Gain deontic over descriptive 5.0 to 41.2 points depending on model; example zero-shot gains +30.1 for gemma-3-12b, +10 for llama-3.3-70b. Models: gemma-3 12B/27B, llama-3.3-70B, olmo-2-32B and others.
limits: Open-weight models 12B-70B. Overlaps with the Wason file in this series.
agent_relevance: Rule type matters. The S0 restatement should record whether a rule is descriptive or deontic, and the check should vary the polarity of the rule.

source: Abi Akl, Gandon, Faron, Monnin (2026) Are you Talking Logic to Me? Assessing Language Models Syllogistic Reasoning Capabilities
finding: Extending FOLIO and P-FOLIO with formal notations shows small language models (fine-tuned or zero-shot) can do as well with formal notations as with natural language while running faster. Adding a short logical definition of the syllogism's category (SEF) to zero-shot prompts boosts small models.
numbers: FOLIO-KR 1204 items; P-FOLIO-KR 301 items; Flan-T5-small and large compared. Accuracy values not extracted.
limits: I read the abstract, setup and dataset tables, not every result table. Small models only.
agent_relevance: Weak evidence that giving a rule definition in context helps small models; test before adopting, likely irrelevant for a large model.

source: Search gap: LLM studies of Byrne-style suppression and probability of conditionals
finding: Several arXiv query forms and two web searches (Byrne suppression, additional or alternative premise, probability of conditionals, affirming the consequent with LLMs) found no paper testing language models on Byrne (1989) suppression or on the Evans-Over / Oaksford-Chater probability of conditionals. The closest conditional work is Holliday et al. (2024, c16), Wang and Shi (2025, c15) and Abe et al. (2026, c25). Web hits were all human studies (Cariani 2017 reports 35% contravening-MP endorsement vs 99% basic MP; Espino 2020 counterfactual suppression), seen only as search snippets.
numbers: Zero LLM x suppression hits in 4 arXiv query forms and 2 web searches this session.
limits: Absence in these search tools is not proof. Semantic Scholar returned HTTP 429. Human figures are snippet-level and unverified.
agent_relevance: A literature gap and a cheap own experiment: MP and MT with and without an extra Byrne-style premise, scored in our harness.
